guard_patterns.handling: Require a directly accessible official DESNZ or ONS source surface.
Keep territorial, end-user and residence-basis statistics distinct.
Keep national, local-authority, 1x1 km model and parcel geography distinct.
Preserve which greenhouse gases and exclusions apply to each source.
Keep kt CO2e, MtCO2e, tCO2e/km2 and negative removals semantics explicit.
Keep 2005-2024 edition, reference year and revision status explicit.
Distinguish measured/reported point-source inputs from modelled area-source distributions.
Retain published uncertainty and methodology limitations where applicable.
Do not convert national, LA, point-source or 1x1 km evidence into a parcel value without parcel binding evidence.
Every generated control must pass deterministic structure and scope checks before publication.

packages.title: DESNZ 2005-2024 local-authority coverage and exclusions QA
facts: The 2005 to 2024 DESNZ local and regional greenhouse gas publication is an Accredited Official Statistics release.
The local-authority series uses nationally available datasets and provides a time series back to 2005.
The main source families include the UK National Atmospheric Emissions Inventory and DESNZ local-area energy-consumption statistics.
The local-authority release covers carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide emissions within UK borders.
Fluorinated gases are excluded from the local-authority statistics because suitable data are not available to estimate them at local level.
The 2026 release states that fluorinated gases accounted for about 2% of UK-level territorial emissions in 2024.
Aviation, shipping and military transport are excluded from local allocation where there is no obvious basis for assigning the emissions to local areas.
The estimates are intended to identify high-emitting sources, monitor change over time and support local carbon-reduction planning.
The technical report describes the dataset as a spatial disaggregation of the UK Greenhouse Gas Inventory on an end-user basis.
Local-authority statistics are not parcel measurements and must not be presented as parcel-specific emissions.

packages.title: DESNZ large-installation point-source and ETS verification QA
facts: Large industrial installations are mapped using the NAEI point-source database.
The point-source compilation uses fuel and emissions information from installations covered by UK ETS or EU ETS during 2005 to 2024.
The compilation also uses regulated pollution-inventory datasets reported to UK environmental regulators.
For ETS installations, operators provide grid references that support strong location information for point sources.
The technical report states that ETS emissions are reported and verified, while acknowledging variation in monitoring quality.
The uncertainty table assigns a low estimated error to the large-industrial ETS category compared with many modelled area-source categories.
Non-ETS large industrial point sources retain more modelling uncertainty than ETS installations.
Point-source data are designed to represent significant sites and do not contain every small combustion process in the economy.
For several source sectors, point-source totals are lower than national inventory totals because smaller processes are absent from point-source datasets.
A point-source location can support a high-confidence source candidate but is not by itself evidence that a specific land parcel owns or contains all reported emissions.

packages.title: DESNZ point-source scope, matching and residual area-source QA
facts: NAEI point-source emissions are initially calculated on a by-source basis rather than an end-user basis.
For relevant fuel-combustion emissions, an end-user increment can be added to represent upstream fuel-production emissions.
Different regulatory reporting scopes can refer to a furnace, installation or wider site, which creates matching limitations.
Company names in point-source and gas-consumption datasets are not always consistent, so some source matching cannot be absolute.
The technical report notes continuing uncertainty in linking some ETS installations to pollution-inventory records.
Autogeneration can be difficult to distinguish from industrial combustion in point-source data and can distort sector-by-sector comparisons.
Point-source data for fuels widely used in small equipment are expected to cover a smaller share of national emissions than fuels concentrated in large plants.
Mixed sectors combine explicitly mapped point sources with modelled area-source emissions.
For mixed sectors, residual area-source emissions are derived after subtracting the point-source total from the relevant national total and are then spatially distributed.
Residual area-source modelling and point-source matching must remain separate from any later parcel-binding claim.

packages.title: DESNZ employment-based 1×1 km area-source modelling QA
facts: Energy use by smaller non-domestic sites is significant even though these sites are not in the NAEI point-source database.
DESNZ reports that smaller industrial combustion facilities represented about 17% of industrial CO2 emissions in 2024 under the referenced GNFR category.
Consistent site-level energy-consumption data are not available for all smaller non-domestic sites across the UK.
The mapping method therefore uses proxy data on employment and energy use to estimate emissions for smaller facilities.
The method models energy-use distribution at 1×1 km resolution and at Local Authority level.
The Inter-Departmental Business Register input described in the report contains about 2.1 million businesses and covers approximately 99% of UK economic activities.
Business grid references are used to aggregate employee counts to 1×1 km grid cells by SIC sector.
Annual sector fuel-use statistics from DESNZ Energy Consumption in the UK are used as modelling inputs.
A 2025 methodological update introduced ETS and Climate Change Agreement data into industrial energy-consumption estimates and was applied back to 2021.
A 1×1 km model cell is an area-source estimate and must not be converted into a parcel-specific measured value without a separate geometry and attribution step.

packages.title: DESNZ revision, supersession and time-series consistency QA
facts: The 2026 local-authority release recalculated 2005 to 2023 estimates using the methodology applied to the 2024 estimates.
Recalculation is intended to preserve a consistent time series for monitoring changes over time.
The release identifies wastewater, landfill, shipping, agriculture and LULUCF among the sources most affected by current inventory revisions.
Point-source estimates for 2005 to 2024 are subject to continuous improvement when additional data or inventory-method changes become available.
Most point-source values may remain unchanged between editions, while selected sites or years can be revised.
The final UK greenhouse gas series for 1990 to 2024 supersedes previous editions after methodological improvements and new data are applied.
Final UK territorial statistics are presented by source first, then updated with end-user estimates and later SIC breakdowns on the publication schedule.
Source-basis emissions attribute emissions to the sector that directly emits them.
End-user statistics reallocate energy-supply emissions to the users of that energy using a modelling process.
Current-edition values and basis labels must be preserved so earlier or differently defined values are not silently mixed into the 2026 evidence.

packages.title: DESNZ LULUCF local disaggregation and uncertainty QA
facts: The LULUCF methodology uses Local Authority boundary datasets to disaggregate national inventory estimates to local areas.
The 2024 local maps present LULUCF emissions or removals per Local Authority area in tonnes CO2e per square kilometre.
Harvested wood products are excluded from the mapped LULUCF totals because they cannot be mapped in this local methodology.
Published 2024 LULUCF inventory uncertainty ranges vary by activity and are reported as 12% to 197% for CO2.
Published 2024 LULUCF inventory uncertainty ranges are reported as 33% to 92% for CH4.
Published 2024 LULUCF inventory uncertainty ranges are reported as 34% to 158% for N2O.
Additional uncertainty arises when national LULUCF estimates are disaggregated to Local Authority or Protected Landscape scale.
The methodology estimates disaggregation uncertainty around 20% to 30% on decadal timescales and notes that annual uncertainty is probably higher.
Probabilistic land-use-change disaggregation and deforestation identification add spatial and temporal uncertainty in some categories.
Published Local Authority LULUCF uncertainty must not be converted into a parcel-specific confidence score without separate parcel evidence.

facts: The official CSV preview exposes fields for country, region, authority, authority code, calendar year, sector, sub-sector, greenhouse gas, territorial emissions, scope-of-influence emissions, population and area.

packages.title: DESNZ territorial/end-user versus ONS residence-basis boundary QA
facts: Final DESNZ territorial greenhouse gas statistics cover emissions occurring within UK borders.
On a source basis, DESNZ attributes emissions to the sector that directly emits them.
On an end-user basis, DESNZ reallocates energy-supply emissions according to where the energy is ultimately used.
The end-user reallocation is modelled and therefore is not the same measure as directly observed point-source emissions.
The 2005 to 2024 local-authority dataset is derived from territorial inventory sources and uses local spatial-disaggregation methods.

The local-authority publication excludes several categories that cannot be robustly allocated locally, including aviation, shipping, military transport and fluorinated gases as specified by the release.
ONS Environmental Accounts use a residence basis that includes UK residents and UK-registered businesses regardless of whether activity occurs in the UK or overseas.
ONS residence-basis statistics exclude foreign visitors and foreign businesses in the UK, making the residence boundary materially different from DESNZ territorial statistics.
Territorial, end-user and residence-basis figures can all be valid official statistics but are not interchangeable without an explicit basis conversion or comparison.
None of these national or local statistical bases alone supplies a measured emission value for a specific parcel.
